statement: Seven cups all stand upside down. In one move you must turn over exactly two cups. Can all seven ever stand the right way up?

choices.misconception: I found a sequence that turned over most of the cups and assumed the last one could be fixed somehow.
I matched the number of moves to the number of cups without checking whether the target is reachable at all.

choices.text: Yes, but it takes many moves
choices.misconception: I assumed that with enough moves any arrangement can be reached.

choices.text: It depends which two cups you pick
choices.misconception: I thought the choice of which cups to flip could change whether the target is reachable.

hints: Count how many cups face up after each move.
Track the number of upward-facing cups. Every move changes that number by two or by nothing at all, so ask what that does to whether the number is odd or even.
Start with 0 cups up, which is even. Each move changes the count by +2, 0 or -2, so the count stays even forever. Seven is odd, so it can never be reached.

solutions.reliable: Count the cups facing up. At the start that is 0, which is even. A move turns over two cups, so it either adds 2, subtracts 2, or leaves the count unchanged - in every case the count stays even. Since 7 is odd, the target can never be reached, no matter how many moves you make. The transferable idea: find a quantity no move can change, and use it to rule the target out.
solutions.elegant: The parity of the number of upright cups is invariant, and it starts even while the goal is odd, so no sequence of moves connects them.

whyOnTest: Proving something impossible is a different skill from finding an answer, and parity is the first tool students get for it.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
